sections.text: Fulminant Secondary HLH Following EBV Reactivation in an Adult With Trisomy 21 After Teplizumab Treatment for Stage 2 Type 1 Diabetes
OBJECTIVE

Teplizumab delays progression from stage 2 to stage 3 type 1 diabetes (T1D). Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reactivation after teplizumab is usually transient and mild. We report EBV reactivation-associated secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) in an adult with trisomy 21 who was treated with teplizumab.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
We describe the clinical course, virologic testing, histopathology, treatment, and follow-up of a 44-year-old man with trisomy 21 and stage 2 T1D after a 14-day teplizumab course.
RESULTS

Six days after completion of the 14-day teplizumab course, he developed respiratory, hepatic, and renal failure. EBV PCR peaked at >2,000,000 copies/mL; serology confirmed reactivation. Lymph node biopsy showed EBV-associated lymphoproliferation, and criteria for secondary HLH were fulfilled (HScore 238). Dexamethasone and four weekly rituximab doses were associated with clinical, biochemical, and virologic recovery. At 12 months, he remained clinically stable with stage 2 T1D and no insulin treatment.
CONCLUSIONS

This case documents EBV reactivation-associated secondary HLH after teplizumab treatment in a patient with trisomy 21. Causality cannot be established, and the absence of pretreatment EBV PCR limits assessment of whether preexisting EBV DNAemia at treatment initiation contributed to the poor outcome. The observation raises a plausible but unproven host-virus-drug interaction and supports early EBV PCR and HLH evaluation after severe inflammatory deterioration after teplizumab.
Graphical Abstract
CASE REPORT

Teplizumab is a non–Fc receptor-binding anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody that delays progression from stage 2 to stage 3 type 1 diabetes (T1D). A 44-year-old man with trisomy 21 and stage 2 T1D received a standard 14-day teplizumab course (Supplementary Fig. 1). Stage 2 T1D had been identified ∼80 months earlier with multiple positive islet autoantibodies (namely, GADA, IA-2A, and ZnT8A) and dysglycemia (e.g., increased fasting plasma glucose 112 mg/dL [6.2 mmol/L], HbA1c 6.4% [46 mmol/mol], normal 2-h plasma glucose on oral glucose tolerance testing); there were no clinical symptoms or other criteria for stage 3 disease. Relevant coexisting conditions included repaired tetralogy of Fallot, hypothyroidism, prior Meckel diverticulum resection, and varicosis. EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgG and EBNA-1 IgG were positive, and EBV VCA IgM was negative before treatment. EBV PCR was not performed immediately before teplizumab administration. Before teplizumab, the patient was clinically well and his diabetes managed without insulin. On history and examination, there was no fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or evidence of active infection. During treatment, he had transient low-grade fever on day 8, a brief increase in C-reactive protein level, lymphopenia below 0.5 × 109/L for 5 days, and mild aminotransferase elevation (Supplementary Fig. 2).

Six days after the final infusion, the patient developed high-grade fever and rapidly progressive, sepsis-like multiorgan dysfunction (Supplementary Fig. 1). He required intensive care for about 12 days because of respiratory failure and shock. Coagulopathy was complicated by severe epistaxis. He developed acute liver failure with hyperammonemia and stage 3 acute kidney injury; hypervolemic decompensation occurred in the setting of renal failure, inflammatory capillary leak, and intensive care fluid management. Renal replacement therapy was required for ∼2 weeks, initially as continuous hemofiltration followed by intermittent dialysis, and renal recovery was achieved. Bilateral pleural effusions required drainage; pleural-fluid cytology was macrophage-rich with mature lymphocytes and no atypical aggregates. Quantitative EBV PCR peaked at >2,000,000 copies/mL. During the episode, serology showed VCA IgM negativity, VCA IgG level of 554 units/mL, and EBNA-1 IgG level >600 units/mL, consistent with EBV reactivation in a previously infected patient. Serial laboratory evolution is provided in Supplementary Fig. 2.

The syndrome fulfilled several criteria for secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), including fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, bicytopenia (hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL and platelets 89 × 109/L; ferritin 10,478 µg/L; soluble interleukin-2 receptor [sIL-2R/sCD25] 15,420 units/mL; triglycerides 539 mg/dL; and fibrinogen 141 mg/dL) (Supplementary Table 1). The HScore was 238, corresponding to a >98% probability of secondary HLH (Supplementary Table 2). Sepsis-like work-up identified no alternative dominant pathogen or non-EBV explanation. Bone marrow hemophagocytosis and natural killer (NK)-cell function were not examined, and patient-specific cytokine or functional peripheral blood mononuclear cell assays were not available.

Imaging showed persistent supra- and infradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy. Cervical lymph node excision demonstrated a necrotizing, highly proliferative lymphoid infiltrate (Ki-67 >90%) dominated by CD3+/CD5+ T cells with strong CD8 expression and numerous programmed cell death protein 1–positive T cells. The B-cell compartment was CD79a+/CD38+ and largely CD20 negative. EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) in situ hybridization showed abundant EBV-positive cells, highly positive EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA) immunostaining, sparse latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) expression, and no MYC, BCL2, or BCL6 rearrangements upon fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) rearrangement was oligoclonal, whereas T-cell receptor γ showed germline configuration. Expert hematopathology review (W.K.), integrating morphology, immunophenotype, EBER/EBNA/LMP1 staining, FISH, clonality testing, and the clinical course, favored severe EBV-associated immunodysregulatory lymphoproliferation rather than overt lymphoma.

High-dose dexamethasone was administered and, given marked EBV replication with multiorgan dysfunction and EBV-associated lymphoproliferation, rituximab was administered weekly (four doses in total) to target EBV-harboring B cells. Clinical recovery was rapid and sustained, with declining EBV DNAemia, improvement of inflammatory markers, recovery of renal and hepatic function, liberation from respiratory support, and discharge (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). At 12-month follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable with stage 2 T1D (HbA1c 5.9% [41 mmol/mol], fasting plasma glucose 96 mg/dL [5.3 mmol/L], and no insulin treatment).
DISCUSSION

Teplizumab is a disease-modifying therapy for stage 2 T1D. In the pivotal TN-10 prevention trial, 44 patients with stage 2 T1D received teplizumab. Pooled safety data across five controlled clinical studies include data on 609 patients treated with teplizumab and 245 control patients. The usual adverse event profile included transient lymphopenia, rash, mild cytokine release syndrome, and reversible liver enzyme elevations. EBV reactivation, uncommon and usually asymptomatic or mild, was reported in ∼5.1% of teplizumab-treated participants versus 2.4% of control individuals in pooled controlled safety data: in the TN-10 trial, quantifiable EBV DNA occurred at weeks 3–6 after the trial regimen in EBV-seropositive participants, and studies in recent-onset T1D reported EBV viremia ∼2–3 weeks after dosing, which typically resolved without antiviral therapy. Against this background, the timing and severity of the present episode were unusual. Because the patient’s pretreatment serology demonstrated EBV seropositivity, the high-grade EBV DNAemia is best classified as EBV reactivation or expansion rather than primary EBV infection. However, absence of pretreatment EBV PCR means we cannot determine whether EBV DNAemia was completely absent at teplizumab initiation or whether subclinical reactivation was already present.

Trisomy 21 represents a biologically distinct immunologic context that may influence host responses to both viral infection and immune-modulating therapies. Individuals with trisomy 21 exhibit constitutive upregulation of interferon-stimulated gene programs, likely related to gene dosage effects involving interferon receptor loci on chromosome 21. In addition, abnormalities in both innate and adaptive immunity, including impaired cytotoxic lymphocyte function, have been described. These features may contribute to reduced capacity for effective clearance of virally infected cells and a lower threshold for sustained immune activation once viral control is disrupted. This well-established immunological background in trisomy 21 provides a plausible framework for dysregulated responses to EBV (Fig. 1).

Converging vulnerabilities that may lead to EBV-driven hyperinflammation under anti-CD3 therapy in trisomy 21: proposed model. Trisomy 21–associated interferon (IFN) pathway priming and reduced cytotoxic reserve intersect with anti-CD3-mediated attenuation of effective CD8 killing, permitting EBV expansion and sustained antigenic drive, with IFN-γ excess and macrophage activation culminating in secondary HLH.

Hyperinflammation in secondary HLH reflects ineffective elimination of antigen-bearing target cells and persistent activation of T cells and macrophages; EBV is the prototypical trigger when cytotoxic immune control is impaired. The combination of high EBV viral load, EBV-associated lymphoproliferation, fulfilled HLH criteria, and clinical improvement after dexamethasone plus rituximab supports EBV involvement. It does not prove that teplizumab caused EBV reactivation, nor does it exclude contributions from cytokine release, intercurrent infection, critical illness, or the underlying trisomy 21 immune phenotype.

Teplizumab modulates T-cell receptor signaling and has been associated with expansion of regulatory or exhaustion-like CD8+ T-cell phenotypes and changes in autoreactive T-cell repertoires rather than broad immunosuppression in typical hosts. It is conceivable that, in a host with limited cytotoxic reserve, anti-CD3-mediated T-cell modulation could transiently reduce effective control of EBV-infected cells while maintaining antigenic stimulation (Fig. 2).

Schematic diagram of the pathogenesis of EBV-driven secondary HLH under teplizumab (anti-CD3) treatment. Latent EBV infection of B cells undergoes reactivation with viral replication and expansion of EBV-infected B cells. Viral antigen presentation via MHC class I activates CD8+ T cells. Teplizumab, an anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody, induces partial T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling and promotes an exhaustion-like CD8+ phenotype, resulting in reduced effective cytotoxic killing. In the presence of host vulnerability (e.g., trisomy 21 with impaired NK- and CD8-mediated cytotoxicity and an interferon-biased inflammatory state), ineffective viral clearance leads to persistent antigen stimulation. Activated CD8+ T cells produce IFN-γ, which drives macrophage activation. Activated macrophages release proinflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-18. This promotes further CD8+ T-cell IFN-γ production, establishing a cytokine amplification loop because of persistent antigenic stimulation and ineffective killing. Endothelial activation and systemic inflammation contribute to coagulopathy and multiorgan dysfunction. The resulting hyperinflammatory state is characterized clinically by fever, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and organ dysfunction, consistent with secondary HLH. This schematic depicts a proposed, hypothetical mechanism; it is consistent with known biology but is not directly demonstrated by the patient’s samples and should be read as a hypothesis rather than an established pathway. LN, lymph node.

Recent mechanistic studies have reported that EBV serostatus can modify immune responses to teplizumab and may correlate with stronger metabolic benefit in some cohorts. These observations refer to prior EBV exposure, not active viral replication. The case we present here, therefore, should not be interpreted as evidence that EBV-seropositive patients generally have increased risk; rather, it highlights that serostatus, active viral load, and host antiviral capacity are distinct variables that should be analyzed separately.

The current teplizumab (TZIELD) prescribing information recommends testing for active EBV and cytomegalovirus infection before initiation, monitoring lymphocyte counts, and monitoring for viral reactivation for at least 2 months after treatment; it further notes that immunocompromised patients, including those with trisomy 21, may be at increased risk. Our case supports a low threshold for EBV PCR and HLH screening when persistent fever, cytopenias, organ dysfunction, or sepsis-like deterioration occur after teplizumab. Such screening may include complete blood cell count; levels of ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, sIL-2R/sCD25, liver enzymes, and coagulation markers; and quantitative EBV PCR.

The lymph node pathology in the case we report was interpreted by expert review as severe EBV-associated immunodysregulatory lymphoproliferation rather than overt lymphoma, based on the integrated histologic, immunophenotypic, molecular, and clinical findings. Nevertheless, malignant transformation is not definitively ruled out by any single test in this setting; the high proliferative index (Ki-67 >90%) and abnormal IGH pattern warranted continued hematologic surveillance. At 12-month follow-up, there was no clinical, laboratory, or imaging evidence of a lymphoproliferative disorder.

Clinical implications should remain proportionate to a single case. We do not think this report alone establishes exclusion criteria. However, in individuals with known impaired antiviral responses or trisomy 21, teplizumab should prompt careful individualized risk–benefit assessment, explicit evaluation for active herpesvirus replication, and early involvement of clinicians experienced in hyperinflammatory syndromes and immune dysregulation. Complex or atypical courses are best managed in settings with rapid access to immunology or hematology, infectious disease, intensive care, and quantitative viral testing.

In summary, we describe fulminant EBV reactivation-associated secondary HLH shortly after teplizumab treatment of an adult with trisomy 21. Although this single case cannot prove causality, it identifies a clinically actionable safety signal: in susceptible hosts, EBV reactivation after T-cell–modulating therapy may progress beyond transient viremia to life-threatening hyperinflammation. Patients treatment with teplizumab who have persistent fever, cytopenias, liver injury, increasing ferritin or lactate dehydrogenase levels, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia, or increasing EBV DNAemia should be evaluated early, therefore, for secondary HLH. Baseline EBV assessment and targeted post-treatment monitoring may be particularly relevant in individuals with trisomy 21 or other conditions associated with immune dysregulation.
